claim: Humans experience unique physical impairments with potentially large consequences compared to other species.
source: In comparative cross-species perspective, humans experience unique physical impairments with potentially large consequences.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a framing assertion for the study.

claim: Fracture is associated with cessation of hunting among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists.
source: Fracture is associated with cessation of hunting, tree chopping, and walking long distances, but not tool manufacture.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis in the results section.

claim: Fracture is associated with cessation of tree chopping among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists.
source: Fracture is associated with cessation of hunting, tree chopping, and walking long distances, but not tool manufacture.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis in the results section.

claim: Fracture is associated with cessation of walking long distances among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists.
source: Fracture is associated with cessation of hunting, tree chopping, and walking long distances, but not tool manufacture.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis in the results section.

claim: Fracture is not associated with cessation of tool manufacture among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists.
source: Fracture is associated with cessation of hunting, tree chopping, and walking long distances, but not tool manufacture.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis in the results section.

claim: Age-specific productivity losses from hunting cessation associated with fracture are approximately 397 lost kcals/day.
source: Age-specific productivity losses from hunting cessation associated with fracture and lower BMD are substantial: ~397 lost kcals/day, with expected future losses of up to 1.9 million kcals (22% of expected production).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the abstract based on calculations described in the methods and results.

claim: Expected future losses from hunting cessation associated with fracture and lower BMD are up to 1.9 million kcals.
source: Age-specific productivity losses from hunting cessation associated with fracture and lower BMD are substantial: ~397 lost kcals/day, with expected future losses of up to 1.9 million kcals (22% of expected production).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the abstract based on calculations described in the methods and results.

claim: Expected future losses from hunting cessation associated with fracture and lower BMD represent 22% of expected production.
source: Age-specific productivity losses from hunting cessation associated with fracture and lower BMD are substantial: ~397 lost kcals/day, with expected future losses of up to 1.9 million kcals (22% of expected production).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the abstract based on calculations described in the methods and results.

claim: Human hunter-gatherers have lower adult mortality than chimpanzees.
source: Human hunter-gatherers have lower adult mortality than chimpanzees and a significant post-reproductive lifespan (Gurven and Kaplan, 2007; Hill et al., 2007; Kaplan et al., 2010; Kaplan et al., 2000; Wood et al., 2017), which generates ample opportunity for incident degenerative disease and dysfunction (Finch, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Human hunter-gatherers have a significant post-reproductive lifespan.
source: Human hunter-gatherers have lower adult mortality than chimpanzees and a significant post-reproductive lifespan (Gurven and Kaplan, 2007; Hill et al., 2007; Kaplan et al., 2010; Kaplan et al., 2000; Wood et al., 2017), which generates ample opportunity for incident degenerative disease and dysfunction (Finch, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Lower adult mortality and significant post-reproductive lifespan generate ample opportunity for incident degenerative disease and dysfunction.
source: Human hunter-gatherers have lower adult mortality than chimpanzees and a significant post-reproductive lifespan (Gurven and Kaplan, 2007; Hill et al., 2007; Kaplan et al., 2010; Kaplan et al., 2000; Wood et al., 2017), which generates ample opportunity for incident degenerative disease and dysfunction (Finch, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hominins showed greater dietary reliance on difficult-to-acquire resources including hunted game at least two million years ago.
source: Evidence of greater dietary reliance by hominins on difficult-to-acquire resources including hunted game at least two mya (Aiello and Wheeler, 1995; Antón et al., 2014; Thompson et al., 2019; Ungar, 2012) suggests delayed peak skill acquisition in adulthood (Gurven et al., 2006; Kaplan et al., 2000; Koster et al., 2020; Walker et al., 2002), possibly when senescence was already underway.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Greater dietary reliance on difficult-to-acquire resources suggests delayed peak skill acquisition in adulthood.
source: Evidence of greater dietary reliance by hominins on difficult-to-acquire resources including hunted game at least two mya (Aiello and Wheeler, 1995; Antón et al., 2014; Thompson et al., 2019; Ungar, 2012) suggests delayed peak skill acquisition in adulthood (Gurven et al., 2006; Kaplan et al., 2000; Koster et al., 2020; Walker et al., 2002), possibly when senescence was already underway.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Peak skill acquisition in adulthood possibly occurred when senescence was already underway.
source: Evidence of greater dietary reliance by hominins on difficult-to-acquire resources including hunted game at least two mya (Aiello and Wheeler, 1995; Antón et al., 2014; Thompson et al., 2019; Ungar, 2012) suggests delayed peak skill acquisition in adulthood (Gurven et al., 2006; Kaplan et al., 2000; Koster et al., 2020; Walker et al., 2002), possibly when senescence was already underway.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the timing of skill acquisition and senescence.

claim: Functional disability of degenerative origin may hinder hominin foraging in costly ways.
source: Functional disability of degenerative origin may hinder hominin foraging in costly ways.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential consequences of disability.

claim: Hunter-gatherers form social groups of clusters of multi-generational resource-pooling units.
source: The ubiquity among hunter-gatherers to form social groups of clusters of multi-generational resource-pooling units (Kaplan et al., 2009; Migliano et al., 2017), and in base camps at least ~400 kya (Kuhn and Stiner, 2019), may reflect a species-typical strategy of complex cooperation to minimize daily risks, including production shortfalls.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Base camps existed at least 400,000 years ago.
source: The ubiquity among hunter-gatherers to form social groups of clusters of multi-generational resource-pooling units (Kaplan et al., 2009; Migliano et al., 2017), and in base camps at least ~400 kya (Kuhn and Stiner, 2019), may reflect a species-typical strategy of complex cooperation to minimize daily risks, including production shortfalls.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Multi-generational resource-pooling units may reflect a species-typical strategy of complex cooperation to minimize daily risks.
source: The ubiquity among hunter-gatherers to form social groups of clusters of multi-generational resource-pooling units (Kaplan et al., 2009; Migliano et al., 2017), and in base camps at least ~400 kya (Kuhn and Stiner, 2019), may reflect a species-typical strategy of complex cooperation to minimize daily risks, including production shortfalls.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of social organization patterns.

claim: Marked thoracic kyphosis and vertebral disc degeneration are evident in Australopithecus afarensis (AL-288) from approximately 3.2 million years ago.
source: For example, marked thoracic kyphosis and vertebral disc degeneration are evident in Australopithecus afarensis (AL-288) from ~3.2 mya (Cook et al., 1983), as is spondylolisthesis in middle Pleistocene humans (SH-1) from ~430 kya (Bonmatí et al., 2010; also see Trinkaus, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Spondylolisthesis is evident in middle Pleistocene humans (SH-1) from approximately 430,000 years ago.
source: For example, marked thoracic kyphosis and vertebral disc degeneration are evident in Australopithecus afarensis (AL-288) from ~3.2 mya (Cook et al., 1983), as is spondylolisthesis in middle Pleistocene humans (SH-1) from ~430 kya (Bonmatí et al., 2010; also see Trinkaus, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Thoracic kyphosis, vertebral disc degeneration, and spondylolisthesis regularly cause lower back pain, difficulty walking, and carrying or lifting objects among modern clinical patients.
source: These ailments regularly cause lower back pain, difficulty walking, and carrying or lifting objects among modern clinical patients (Francis et al., 2008), who may provide indirect insights into the consequences of disability in past hominin populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Modern clinical patients may provide indirect insights into the consequences of disability in past hominin populations.
source: These ailments regularly cause lower back pain, difficulty walking, and carrying or lifting objects among modern clinical patients (Francis et al., 2008), who may provide indirect insights into the consequences of disability in past hominin populations.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the applicability of modern clinical data to past populations.

claim: Among Yora forager-horticulturalists of Peru, men are unable to forage due to illness or injury on 11% of all days.
source: Among Yora forager-horticulturalists of Peru, men are unable to forage due to illness or injury on 11% of all days (Sugiyama and Chacon, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Among Shiwiar forager-horticulturalists of Ecuador, more than 60% of individuals experience an impairment severe enough to interfere with subsistence work for at least 1 month.
source: Among Shiwiar forager-horticulturalists of Ecuador, >60% of individuals experience an impairment (e.g. chronic pain, fracture, laceration, infection, animal bite or sting, and burn) severe enough to interfere with subsistence work for ≥1 month; bone fractures – a focus of the current study – may be more likely than other impairments to cause prolonged disability (Sugiyama, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Bone fractures may be more likely than other impairments to cause prolonged disability among Shiwiar forager-horticulturalists.
source: Among Shiwiar forager-horticulturalists of Ecuador, >60% of individuals experience an impairment (e.g. chronic pain, fracture, laceration, infection, animal bite or sting, and burn) severe enough to interfere with subsistence work for ≥1 month; bone fractures – a focus of the current study – may be more likely than other impairments to cause prolonged disability (Sugiyama, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists, 75% of adults report being bedridden due to illness or injury at least once in the 3 months prior to survey.
source: Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists of Bolivia, the population studied here, 75% of adults report being bedridden due to illness or injury at least once in the 3 months prior to survey, and Tsimane are incapacitated on about 10% of all days (Gurven et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Tsimane are incapacitated on about 10% of all days.
source: Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists of Bolivia, the population studied here, 75% of adults report being bedridden due to illness or injury at least once in the 3 months prior to survey, and Tsimane are incapacitated on about 10% of all days (Gurven et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Bone mineral density accounts for approximately 70% of the variance in bone strength.
source: bone mineral density (BMD), which accounts for ~70% of the variance in bone strength (NIH Consensus Development Panel on Osteoporosis Prevention, Diagnosis, and Therapy, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Thoracic vertebral deformity is regularly observed in diverse hominin skeletal samples.
source: Thoracic vertebral deformity is regularly observed in diverse hominin skeletal samples (Chapman, 1972; Cook et al., 1983; Dequeker et al., 1997; Foldes et al., 1995; Gresky et al., 2016; Lieverse et al., 2007; Mays, 1996; Trinkaus, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Thoracic vertebral fractures are among the most common fragility fractures in humans living in post-industrialized populations.
source: Thoracic vertebral fractures are also among the most common fragility fractures in humans living in post-industrialized populations (Sambrook and Cooper, 2006), and are more common among Tsimane compared to age- and sex-matched US (Los Angeles) controls (Stieglitz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Thoracic vertebral fractures are more common among Tsimane compared to age- and sex-matched US (Los Angeles) controls.
source: Thoracic vertebral fractures are also among the most common fragility fractures in humans living in post-industrialized populations (Sambrook and Cooper, 2006), and are more common among Tsimane compared to age- and sex-matched US (Los Angeles) controls (Stieglitz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Spontaneous vertebral fractures have not been observed in other great apes, even in individuals with severe osteopenia.
source: While other great apes experience degenerative disease (Jurmain, 2000; Lovell, 1990), spontaneous vertebral fractures have not been observed in other apes, even in individuals with severe osteopenia (Gunji et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Bipedal hominins appear to be especially susceptible to fragility fractures of the spine.
source: Bipedal hominins thus appear to be especially susceptible to fragility fractures of the spine (Cotter et al., 2011) and perhaps other anatomical regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and inference from comparative data.

claim: Most activities of daily living generate vertebral loads.
source: One might expect considerable productivity loss associated with compromised human thoracic vertebral body strength, as most activities of daily living (e.g. sitting, walking, running, lifting, and even breathing) generate vertebral loads (Myers and Wilson, 1997; Polga et al., 2004; Rohlmannt et al., 2001; Stewart and Hall, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: For many common activities, the greatest spinal compressive loads are generated in the thoracolumbar region.
source: For many common activities (e.g. neutral standing, standing with weight, mild trunk flexion and extension, and lifting objects above the head) the greatest spinal compressive loads are generated in the thoracolumbar region (Bruno et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Tsimane are semi-sedentary forager-horticulturalists inhabiting more than 90 villages in lowland Bolivia.
source: Tsimane are semi-sedentary forager-horticulturalists inhabiting >90 villages in lowland Bolivia.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the study population.

claim: The household is the basic economic unit for production and consumption among Tsimane.
source: The household is the basic economic unit for production and consumption, and most daily coordination is confined to the nuclear and extended family.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about Tsimane social organization.

claim: Tsimane men hunt about once every week or two on average.
source: On average, men hunt about once every week or two; hunting is more common during the wet season and in interior forest villages.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about Tsimane hunting behavior.

claim: The average Tsimane hunt lasts 8.4 hours and covers 17.9 km.
source: The average hunt lasts 8.4 hr and covers 17.9 km (Trumble et al., 2014) and often involves carrying animal carcasses long distances.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Much of the protein and fat consumed by Tsimane come from hunting and fishing.
source: Much of the protein and fat consumed by Tsimane come from hunting and fishing (Kraft et al., 2018), whereas most (62%) of the total calories in the diet come from cultigens grown in small swiddens.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Most (62%) of the total calories in the Tsimane diet come from cultigens grown in small swiddens.
source: Much of the protein and fat consumed by Tsimane come from hunting and fishing (Kraft et al., 2018), whereas most (62%) of the total calories in the diet come from cultigens grown in small swiddens.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Tsimane women's physical activity level is in the 'moderate to active' range (PAL = 1.7–1.9) and is constant throughout adulthood.
source: Women's physical activity level (PAL; defined as the ratio of total daily energy expenditure to daily basal metabolism) is in the 'moderate to active' range (PAL = 1.7–1.9) and is constant throughout adulthood.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about Tsimane women's activity levels.

claim: Tsimane men's physical activity level is 'vigorously active' (PAL = 2.0–2.2) and declines by 10–20% from the peak in the late 20s to older adulthood (age 60+ years).
source: Men's PAL is 'vigorously active' (PAL = 2.0–2.2) and declines by 10–20% from the peak (in the late 20s) to older adulthood (age 60+ years) (Gurven et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Physical strength peaks in the mid-to-late 20s among Tsimane, then declines thereafter, reaching approximately 60% of maximum adult capacity by age 70.
source: Physical strength peaks in the mid-to-late 20s, then declines thereafter, reaching ~60% of maximum adult capacity by age 70 (Gurven et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Compared to Los Angeles matched controls, age-standardized prevalence of thoracic vertebral body fracture is two times higher for Tsimane women and 3.3 times higher for men.
source: Compared to more sedentary Los Angeles matched controls, age-standardized prevalence of thoracic vertebral body fracture is two times higher for Tsimane women and 3.3 times higher for men using directly comparable CT methods (Stieglitz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: For Tsimane adults aged 50+, 38% experience some movement restriction.
source: For adults aged 50+, 38% experience some movement restriction (e.g. during flexion or extension), most commonly in the dorsolumbar, hip, knee, or shoulder regions.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the study population.

claim: Nearly 70% of Tsimane adults aged 50+ are clinically diagnosed with some condition of the musculoskeletal system and connective tissue.
source: Nearly 70% of adults aged 50+ are also clinically diagnosed with some condition of the musculoskeletal system and connective tissue (i.e. codes M00–M99 using the International Classification of Diseases version 10) by Tsimane Health and Life History Project (THLHP) physicians.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the study population based on clinical diagnoses.

claim: The Tsimane thoracic CT sample includes all individuals who self-identified as Tsimane and who were aged 40+ at study enrollment (n = 493).
source: The Tsimane thoracic CT sample used to measure thoracic vertebral body BMD and fracture presence and severity includes all individuals who met the inclusion criteria of self-identifying as Tsimane and who were aged 40+ at study enrollment (mean ± SD age = 55.9 ± 9.9, age range: 41–91 years, 48% female, n = 493)
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: The Tsimane CT sample is thought to be representative of all Tsimane aged 40+ years.
source: This CT sample is thought to be representative of all Tsimane aged 40+ years .
evidence: This is a statement about the representativeness of the study sample.

claim: CT-derived vertebral body BMD estimates are highly accurate and strongly positively correlated (Pearson r's > 0.9) with ash weight of dry bone.
source: CT-derived vertebral body BMD estimates are highly accurate and strongly positively correlated (Pearson r's > 0.9) with ash weight of dry bone (Ho et al., 1990; Reinbold et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CT-derived thoracic vertebral body BMD measure is strongly positively correlated (Pearson r's > 0.9) with CT-derived lumbar vertebral body BMD measures.
source: This CT-derived thoracic vertebral body BMD measure is strongly positively correlated (Pearson r's > 0.9) with CT-derived lumbar vertebral body BMD measures (Budoff et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Phantomless BMD estimates correlate strongly (Pearson r = 0.99) with standard phantom-based CT BMD estimates.
source: Phantomless BMD estimates correlate strongly (Pearson r = 0.99) with standard phantom-based CT BMD estimates (Budoff et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Genant's semi-quantitative technique provides highly reproducible diagnosis of fractures and is currently the most widely used clinical technique for identifying and diagnosing fracture.
source: While there is no consensus regarding the radiologic definition of vertebral fracture, the GST provides highly reproducible diagnosis of fractures and is currently the most widely used clinical technique for identifying and diagnosing fracture (Shepherd et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Prevalence of any thoracic vertebral body fracture (grade ≥1) for Tsimane men aged 40+ years is 36% (95% CI: 30–42).
source: Prevalence of any thoracic vertebral body fracture (i.e. grade ≥1; including mild, moderate, or severe) for men aged 40+ years is 36% (95% CI: 30–42) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study data, also shown in Figure 2.

claim: Using a more conservative fracture definition (grade ≥2), Tsimane men's fracture prevalence is 11% (95% CI: 7–15).
source: Using a more conservative fracture definition (i.e. grade ≥2; including only moderate or severe), men's prevalence is 11% (95% CI: 7–15).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study data.

claim: Neither Tsimane men's age nor thoracic vertebral body BMD is significantly associated with fracture risk.
source: Neither men's age nor thoracic vertebral body BMD is significantly associated with fracture risk (Figure 2), regardless of fracture grade.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study data, also shown in Figure 2.

claim: Prevalence of any grade 1 fracture for Tsimane women aged 40+ years is 19% (95% CI: 14–24).
source: Prevalence of any grade 1 fracture for women aged 40+ years is 19% (95% CI: 14–24) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study data, also shown in Figure 3.

claim: Tsimane women's grade 2 fracture prevalence is 7% (95% CI: 4–10).
source: Women's grade 2 fracture prevalence is 7% (95% CI: 4–10).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study data.

claim: Tsimane women's age does not significantly predict fracture risk in univariate models, regardless of fracture grade.
source: Women's age does not significantly predict fracture risk in univariate models, regardless of fracture grade.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study data.

claim: BMD is inversely associated with Tsimane women's fracture risk after adjusting for age.
source: BMD is inversely associated with women's fracture risk after adjusting for age (grade 1: adjusted relative riskBMD per SD increase=0.49, 95% CI: 0.34–0.72, p<0.001; grade 2: adjusted relative riskBMD per SD increase=0.25, 95% CI: 0.11–0.57, p=0.001; see Figure 3)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study data, also shown in Figure 3.

claim: Thirty-eight percent of Tsimane men with fracture (grade ≥1) ceased hunting, compared to 13% with no fracture.
source: Thirty-eight percent of men with fracture (grade ≥1) ceased hunting, compared to 13% with no fracture (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study data, also shown in Table 1.

claim: After adjusting for age, odds of hunting cessation are 7.3 times greater (95% CI: 3.3–17.6, p<0.001, FDR q < 0.001) for Tsimane men with vs. without fracture.
source: After adjusting for age, odds of hunting cessation are 7.3 times greater (95% CI: 3.3–17.6, p<0.001, FDR q < 0.001, n = 256) for men with vs. without fracture (Appendix 1—table 3: Model 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study data.

claim: Men with fracture under-produce to a lesser extent at younger vs. older ages because of high hunting participation rates by younger men regardless of fracture status.
source: Men with fracture under-produce to a lesser extent at younger vs. older ages because of high hunting participation rates by younger men regardless of fracture status (Table 1 and Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the study data.

claim: At age 61, Tsimane men with fracture produce 481 fewer hunting kcals/day than men without fracture (1007 vs. 526 kcals/day, respectively).
source: As hunting cessation becomes increasingly likely with age, particularly for men with fracture, daily productivity losses associated with fracture (i.e. the hunting productivity differential for men with vs. without fracture) increase until age 61, when men with fracture produce 481 fewer hunting kcals/day than men without fracture (1007 vs. 526 kcals/day, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations.

claim: The loss of 481 hunting kcals/day at age 61 represents 19% of the mean daily per-capita energy intake for a Tsimane man that age (2592 kcals).
source: This loss of 481 kcals/day – the equivalent of 120 g of protein (or 53 g of fat) – represents 19% of the mean daily per-capita energy intake for a Tsimane man that age (2592 kcals), and 52% of the mean intake from protein and fat (919 kcals).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations.

claim: The loss of 481 hunting kcals/day at age 61 represents 52% of the mean intake from protein and fat (919 kcals) for a Tsimane man that age.
source: This loss of 481 kcals/day – the equivalent of 120 g of protein (or 53 g of fat) – represents 19% of the mean daily per-capita energy intake for a Tsimane man that age (2592 kcals), and 52% of the mean intake from protein and fat (919 kcals).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations.

claim: The loss of 481 hunting kcals/day at age 61 exceeds daily fishing production at that age by 171 kcals.
source: By comparison, this loss of 481 hunting kcals/day at age 61 exceeds daily fishing production at that age by 171 kcals (based on men's observed age-specific daily fishing production [see Materials and methods and Figure 4]).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations, also shown in Figure 4.

claim: Daily hunting productivity losses associated with fracture exceed fishing productivity for 14 years, from ages 55 to 68 (by 29–171 kcals/day).
source: Daily hunting productivity losses associated with fracture exceed fishing productivity for 14 years, from ages 55 to 68 (by 29–171 kcals/day).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations.

claim: To wholly offset hunting productivity losses, a Tsimane man would have to fish an additional 51–76 min/day in the age range 55-68.
source: In this same age range, based on observed age-specific return rates and time allocation, to wholly offset hunting productivity losses a Tsimane man would have to fish an additional 51–76 min/day (e.g. from an observed 49 to an expected 125 fishing min/day at age 61 [an increase of 155%]; assuming identical fishing return rates regardless of fracture status and BMD; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations.

claim: Future productivity losses associated with fracture peak at age 40, when Tsimane men with fracture can expect to lose 1.15 million kcals over their remaining life.
source: Future productivity losses associated with fracture (i.e. the hunting productivity differential for men with vs. without fracture) peak at age 40, when men with fracture can expect to lose 1.15 million kcals over their remaining life; at that age, this loss represents 14% of men's total future hunting production (8.49 million kcals).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations.

claim: At age 40, the future productivity loss of 1.15 million kcals represents 14% of Tsimane men's total future hunting production (8.49 million kcals).
source: Future productivity losses associated with fracture (i.e. the hunting productivity differential for men with vs. without fracture) peak at age 40, when men with fracture can expect to lose 1.15 million kcals over their remaining life; at that age, this loss represents 14% of men's total future hunting production (8.49 million kcals).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations.

claim: Future hunting productivity losses associated with fracture exceed future fishing productivity for 16 years, from ages 49 to 64 (by 2–32% or 4772–96,419 expected cumulative future kcals).
source: Future hunting productivity losses associated with fracture exceed future fishing productivity for 16 years, from ages 49 to 64 (by 2–32% [or 4772–96,419 expected cumulative future kcals]; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations, also shown in Figure 4.

claim: Peak hunting productivity losses for Tsimane men with fracture and lower BMD vs. men without fracture and higher BMD occur at age 60 with a loss of 650 kcals/day.
source: In this case, peak losses at a given age (age 60: 650 kcals/day – the equivalent of 163 g of protein [or 72 g of fat]) represent 25% of the mean daily per-capita energy intake for a Tsimane man that age and 70% of the mean intake from protein and fat.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations.

claim: Peak hunting productivity losses at age 60 (650 kcals/day) represent 25% of the mean daily per-capita energy intake for a Tsimane man that age.
source: In this case, peak losses at a given age (age 60: 650 kcals/day – the equivalent of 163 g of protein [or 72 g of fat]) represent 25% of the mean daily per-capita energy intake for a Tsimane man that age and 70% of the mean intake from protein and fat.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations.

claim: Peak hunting productivity losses at age 60 (650 kcals/day) represent 70% of the mean intake from protein and fat for a Tsimane man that age.
source: In this case, peak losses at a given age (age 60: 650 kcals/day – the equivalent of 163 g of protein [or 72 g of fat]) represent 25% of the mean daily per-capita energy intake for a Tsimane man that age and 70% of the mean intake from protein and fat.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations.

claim: Forty-six percent of Tsimane men with fracture ceased chopping trees, compared to 21% with no fracture.
source: Forty-six percent of men with fracture ceased chopping trees, compared to 21% with no fracture (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study data, also shown in Table 2.

claim: After adjusting for age, odds of tree chopping cessation are 6.9 times greater (95% CI: 3.1–16.6, p<0.001, FDR q < 0.001) for Tsimane men with vs. without fracture.
source: After adjusting for age, odds of tree chopping cessation are 6.9 times greater (95% CI: 3.1–16.6, p<0.001, FDR q < 0.001, n = 256) for men with vs. without fracture (Appendix 1—table 6: Model 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study data.

claim: Twenty percent of Tsimane women with fracture ceased weaving, compared to 13% with no fracture.
source: Twenty percent of women with fracture ceased weaving, compared to 13% with no fracture (Table 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study data, also shown in Table 3.

claim: After adjusting for age, odds of weaving cessation are not significantly associated with fracture among Tsimane women.
source: After adjusting for age, odds of weaving cessation are not significantly associated with fracture (adjusted ORFracture = 2.2, 95% CI: 0.8–6.4, p=0.129, FDR q = 0.172, n = 237, Appendix 1—table 7: Model 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study data.

claim: Weaving is the only task examined for which fracture is not associated with compromised participation.
source: Weaving is the only task examined for which fracture is not associated with compromised participation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study findings.

claim: Sixty-nine percent of Tsimane adults with fracture are unable to walk a full day, compared to 38% with no fracture.
source: Sixty-nine percent of adults with fracture are unable to walk a full day, compared to 38% with no fracture (Table 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study data, also shown in Table 4.

claim: After adjusting for age and sex, odds of inability to walk all day are 8.2 times greater (95% CI: 4.8–14.5, p<0.001, FDR q < 0.001) for Tsimane adults with vs. without fracture.
source: After adjusting for age and sex, odds of inability to walk all day are 8.2 times greater (95% CI: 4.8–14.5, p<0.001, FDR q < 0.001, n = 493) for adults with vs. without fracture (Appendix 1—table 9: Model 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study data.

claim: Tsimane men with fracture are more likely than men without fracture to report mobility limitations due to hip problems as a reason for hunting and tree chopping cessation.
source: Men with fracture are more likely than men without fracture to report mobility limitations due to hip problems as a reason for hunting and tree chopping cessation (Appendix 1—tables 10 and 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the study data.

claim: Among Tsimane men who ceased hunting and tree chopping, men with fracture are younger, on average, than men without fracture.
source: This is noteworthy because among men who ceased hunting and tree chopping, men with fracture are younger, on average, than men without fracture, and all else equal one expects younger men to be less likely than older men to report hip problems (for men ceasing hunting: mean age by fracture status = 63 vs. 68; for men ceasing tree chopping: mean age = 62 vs. 68).
evidence: This is a finding from the study data.

claim: Trabecular bone losses during adulthood are not fully regained.
source: Substantial cumulative future productivity losses may be expected from compromised vertebral body strength because trabecular bone losses during adulthood are not fully regained (Mosekilde, 1989; Mosekilde et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spinal fracture may impede daily subsistence activities for the remainder of life once it occurs.
source: Once spinal fracture occurs it may impede daily subsistence activities for the remainder of life.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the long-term consequences of fracture.

claim: Tsimane thoracic vertebral fractures appear to result from both trauma and senescence.
source: Tsimane thoracic vertebral fractures appear to result from both trauma and senescence (Stieglitz et al., 2019) and are not just prevalent among the oldest adults (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Tsimane thoracic vertebral fractures are not just prevalent among the oldest adults.
source: Tsimane thoracic vertebral fractures appear to result from both trauma and senescence (Stieglitz et al., 2019) and are not just prevalent among the oldest adults (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Tsimane women's thoracic vertebral body BMD is inversely associated with thoracic vertebral body fracture risk.
source: Tsimane women's thoracic vertebral body BMD is inversely associated with thoracic vertebral body fracture risk, suggesting a role of compromised bone strength in precipitating fracture.
evidence: This is a finding from the study data.

claim: High reproductive effort is associated with reduced bone strength for Tsimane women.
source: High reproductive effort (i.e. early onset of reproduction, on-demand breastfeeding, short interbirth intervals, and high parity) is associated with reduced bone strength for Tsimane women (Stieglitz et al., 2015a; Stieglitz et al., 2019) and may thus constrain the ability of bone tissue to respond to mechanical loading from a physically active lifestyle.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Intimate partner violence against Tsimane women is prevalent, particularly among younger women.
source: However, intimate partner violence against women is prevalent (Stieglitz et al., 2018), particularly among younger women, and may precipitate traumatic fracture at diverse skeletal sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Average production deficits from hunting cessation are 261 lost hunting kcals/day for Tsimane men with vs. without fracture, averaging from ages 40 to 74 years.
source: Energetic deficits are substantial, averaging from ages 40 to 74 years 261 lost hunting kcals/day for men with vs. without fracture (Figure 4 and Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations, also shown in Figure 4.

claim: Average production deficits are 397 lost hunting kcals/day for Tsimane men with both fracture and lower BMD vs. men without fracture and higher BMD.
source: Average production deficits are even greater for men with both fracture and lower BMD (vs. men without fracture and higher BMD): 397 lost hunting kcals/day, equivalent to 15% of the mean daily per-capita energy intake, and 44% of the mean intake from protein and fat (Kraft et al., 2018; Figure 5 and Appendix 1—table 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study calculations, also shown in Figure 5.

claim: Adults in Western industrialized settings with musculoskeletal problems show productivity losses of 10–15% for frequent computer users across various industries.
source: By crude comparison, adults in Western industrialized settings with musculoskeletal problems show productivity losses of 10–15% for frequent computer users across various industries (Hagberg et al., 2002) and up to 28% for construction workers with more physically demanding jobs (Meerding et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adults in Western industrialized settings with musculoskeletal problems show productivity losses of up to 28% for construction workers with more physically demanding jobs.
source: By crude comparison, adults in Western industrialized settings with musculoskeletal problems show productivity losses of 10–15% for frequent computer users across various industries (Hagberg et al., 2002) and up to 28% for construction workers with more physically demanding jobs (Meerding et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: For osteoporotic adults aged 50+ years in the Netherlands, the cost of clinical spine fracture in terms of work absenteeism exceeds 25% of the mean annual income.
source: For osteoporotic adults aged 50+ years in the Netherlands, the cost of clinical spine fracture in terms of work absenteeism exceeds 25% of the mean annual income (Eekman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Tsimane age-specific energetic deficits peak in the early 60s.
source: Tsimane age-specific energetic deficits peak in the early 60s (Figures 4 and 5 and Appendix 1—tables 4 and 5), which is near the age at which Tsimane adults achieve peak numbers of dependent offspring and grand offspring (Gurven and Kaplan, 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from the study calculations shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The early 60s is near the age at which Tsimane adults achieve peak numbers of dependent offspring and grand offspring.
source: Tsimane age-specific energetic deficits peak in the early 60s (Figures 4 and 5 and Appendix 1—tables 4 and 5), which is near the age at which Tsimane adults achieve peak numbers of dependent offspring and grand offspring (Gurven and Kaplan, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Aging Tsimane women may maintain peak or near-peak subsistence involvement with relatively minimal disability-related productivity losses, despite increasing frailty.
source: Given the ubiquity across subsistence populations of the sexual division of labor, with men typically focusing on high strength tasks, aging women may maintain peak or near-peak subsistence involvement with relatively minimal disability-related productivity losses, despite increasing frailty.
evidence: This is an inference from the study findings about sex differences in task requirements.

claim: In industrialized populations, severe thoracolumbar vertebral deformity is more strongly associated with functional impairments for men than women.
source: Relatedly, in industrialized populations there is some evidence from population-based cohorts that severe thoracolumbar vertebral deformity is more strongly associated with functional impairments for men than women (Burger et al., 1997), perhaps because men load their spines more heavily.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Men may load their spines more heavily than women, which may explain why severe thoracolumbar vertebral deformity is more strongly associated with functional impairments for men.
source: Relatedly, in industrialized populations there is some evidence from population-based cohorts that severe thoracolumbar vertebral deformity is more strongly associated with functional impairments for men than women (Burger et al., 1997), perhaps because men load their spines more heavily.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed sex differences.

claim: Fishing is an important source of protein and fat for Tsimane.
source: Fishing is also an important source of protein and fat for Tsimane (Gurven et al., 2013; Hooper, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tsimane cognitive function is generally well preserved throughout adulthood among both schooled and non-schooled adults.
source: Tsimane cognitive function is generally well preserved throughout adulthood among both schooled and non-schooled adults (Gurven et al., 2017a), consistent with a late-life service niche emphasizing information transmission of accumulated wisdom, experience, and judgment.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Preserved cognitive function is consistent with a late-life service niche emphasizing information transmission of accumulated wisdom, experience, and judgment.
source: Tsimane cognitive function is generally well preserved throughout adulthood among both schooled and non-schooled adults (Gurven et al., 2017a), consistent with a late-life service niche emphasizing information transmission of accumulated wisdom, experience, and judgment.
evidence: This is an inference connecting cognitive preservation to social roles.

claim: Extant hunter-gatherers with relatively minimal acculturation exhibit a modal adult lifespan of 68–78 years.
source: Extensive longevity may be a novel life history feature of modern H. sapiens that was absent among prior hominin species; extant hunter-gatherers with relatively minimal acculturation exhibit a modal adult lifespan of 68–78 years (Gurven and Kaplan, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Extensive longevity may be a novel life history feature of modern H. sapiens that was absent among prior hominin species.
source: Extensive longevity may be a novel life history feature of modern H. sapiens that was absent among prior hominin species; extant hunter-gatherers with relatively minimal acculturation exhibit a modal adult lifespan of 68–78 years (Gurven and Kaplan, 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about hominin evolution.

claim: Estimates of disability-related productivity loss may be more relevant for understanding lifeways of past hominin populations with life histories similar to modern H. sapiens.
source: It is thus possible that our estimates of disability-related productivity loss are more relevant for understanding lifeways of past hominin populations with more similar life histories as modern H. sapiens and perhaps some archaic humans (e.g. H. heidelbergensis), but less applicable to Lower Paleolithic and earlier hominins with shorter adult lifespans.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Ache hunters cite fear of disability as an important reason why they willingly conform to band-wide conventions of need-based food sharing.
source: Perhaps not surprisingly, Ache hunters cite fear of disability as an important reason why they willingly conform to band-wide conventions of need-based food sharing (Hill and Hurtado, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Individuals may have survived periods of prolonged disability only via costly provisioning and care by others.
source: It has been proposed that individuals may have survived periods of prolonged disability only via costly provisioning and care by others (Gurven et al., 2000; Sugiyama and Chacon, 2000), although the extent to which others adjust their activity budgets, food production, and sharing to compensate for disability-related productivity loss is beyond the scope of the present study.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vertebral deformities are observed in diverse hominin skeletal samples yet the social and behavioral implications of these deformities remain obscure.
source: Vertebral deformities are observed in diverse hominin skeletal samples yet the social and behavioral implications of these deformities remain obscure.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Bone properties may represent a potential proxy for inferring behavioral consequences of skeletal deformity in prior hominin populations.
source: In the absence of direct evidence of disability-related productivity loss in the fossil record, bone properties may represent a potential proxy for inferring behavioral consequences of skeletal deformity in prior hominin populations.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential use of bone properties as proxies.

claim: Studies of contemporary small-scale subsistence populations like the Tsimane can offer a unique opportunity to examine potential consequences of skeletal deformity in a population-representative adult sample.
source: While our ability to make inferences about the past using data collected in contemporary populations is limited, studies of contemporary small-scale subsistence populations like the Tsimane can offer a unique opportunity to examine potential consequences of skeletal deformity in a population-representative adult sample.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of the study approach.

claim: The present study provides a framework for interpreting morphological signals identified in the fossil record.
source: The present study provides a framework for interpreting morphological signals identified in the fossil record; while this study is narrowly focused on specific morphological features, and while it overlooks important subsistence tasks performed by women, it can nonetheless be an exemplar for future ethno-archaeological inquiry into potential economic and social consequences of disability in past human populations.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the study.
